homework.book_ref: Let's fill the above information in this table, p.205
homework.description: Fill in the frequency table: Subjects (M, L, T, P.E., A) against number of children who like each subject the most.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the scenario: two classmates want to find the most liked subject and wrote different questions. Students read Look at the questions asked by Rohan and Anjali, p.203 ("Tick the question that is the most appropriate for finding the 'most liked subject'....") and discuss in pairs which question would give comparable, countable answers. Pairs share reasoning with the class.

Students turn to the raw list of 45 responses and work on Look at the children's responses above and answer the following questions, p.204 ("Fill in: the number of children who like Mathematics...."). They scan and count responses for each subject, recording counts on their slates or books, experiencing directly how effortful scanning an unorganised list is.

Teacher presents the side-by-side view of Way 1 (raw list) and Way 2 (frequency table). Students tackle Now look at the above table and answer the following questions, p.205 ("Identify the most common and least common favourite subject...."), identifying peaks and comparing the two formats. The class discusses why a table makes comparison quicker; teacher draws out the key insight without giving it away.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often tick Rohan's open question as correct because it feels friendlier — press them to explain what answers it would produce and whether those answers could be easily counted. T-3 (filling the blank frequency table) covers the same tallying procedure as T-2 and is equally valid as reinforcement at home.
materials: Slates or rough paper for tallying

section_titles: Reading and interpreting a pictograph (Colourful Golas)
periods.activity_title: Reading Pictures as Data: The Colourful Golas Pictograph

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Look at the information given above, p.206
tasks_in_class.description: Colour the outline drawings of golas to match the colours shown in Rohan's and Anjali's data records.
Which colour ice gola do the children eat (a) the most and (b) the least? How do you know?
Which colour golas did boys eat the most?
Which of the ways of representing data did you use to answer these questions and why?

time_bands.activity: Students open to p.206 and complete Look at the information given above, p.206 ("Colour the outline drawings of golas to match the colours shown in Rohan's and Anjali's data records."). The colouring act orients students to what the two records show before any question is asked.

Students work on Q1, p.206 ("Which colour ice gola do the children eat (a) the most and (b) the least? How do you know?") by counting icons in Anjali's and Rohan's pictographs. Teacher circulates asking 'how do you know?' to push students to cite icon counts, not guesses.

Students answer Q3, p.207 ("Which colour golas did boys eat the most?"), switching to Rohan's representation which separates boys' and girls' icons. Teacher prompts: which record was easier to use for this question and why?

Class discussion on Q5, p.207 ("Which of the ways of representing data did you use to answer these questions and why?"). Students articulate that different questions call for different representations — a whole-group moment that consolidates the section.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is reading both pictographs as equivalent and ignoring which one separates boys from girls — Q3 and Q4 can only be answered from Rohan's record; redirect students who try to use Anjali's. Q2 (Anjali and Rohan's personal preference) and Q4 (girls' preference) follow the same icon-counting procedure as Q1 and Q3 respectively and can be set as additional practice: Q2 p.206 and Q4 p.207.
materials: Coloured pencils or crayons (orange, green, yellow, red, blue)

section_titles: Collecting and organising data in a two-way table (Chess or Cricket)
periods.activity_title: Our Class Surveys Itself: The Chess or Cricket Two-Way Table

tasks_in_class.description: Find out from your classmates how many of them play only chess, only cricket, both or neither. Record in the space provided.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Now let us organise the above data in the table, p.207
tasks_in_class.description: Fill the two-way table: rows Chess only / Cricket only / Both / Neither; columns No. of Girls and No. of Boys.
Answer: (1) Who plays Chess the most — Boys or Girls? (2) Who plays Cricket the most — Boys or Girls? (3) How many children play both types of games?

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the four categories — chess only, cricket only, both, neither — and models how to record a single response. Students plan how to move around the class and ask without confusion, agreeing on a simple tally system.

Students conduct Activity — Chess or Cricket, p.207 ("Find out from your classmates how many of them play only chess, only cricket, both or neither...."), moving around the room in pairs to collect responses and keeping a tally on rough paper, separating girls' and boys' responses.

Students return to their seats and complete Now let us organise the above data in the table, p.207 ("Fill the two-way table: rows Chess only / Cricket only / Both / Neither; columns No. of Girls and No. of Boys."), transferring their tallies into the structured two-way table.

Students answer Answer these questions, p.207 ("Who plays Chess the most — Boys or Girls?....") using their own table. A brief class share-out surfaces any discrepancies between groups' counts and teacher leads a discussion on why the table makes comparison across gender and game type straightforward.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes count a child who plays 'both' in both the chess-only and cricket-only rows — emphasise that 'both' is its own separate row. Where class numbers are small, the activity still works; if a category has zero responses, students should write 0, not leave it blank.
materials: Rough paper or slates for tallying during the survey

section_titles: Reading a pictograph and computing totals (Bal Mela)
periods.activity_title: Bal Mela Sales: Reading Pictographs and Computing Totals

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the table: total sold items for Fruit Chaats and Sandwiches across all three days.
On which day were the most sandwiches sold?
Which item had the highest sale on Day 2?
Complete the total sales table (Day 1, Day 2, Day 3 combined) and circle the day that had the highest sales.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws attention to the two Bal Mela pictographs on p.208 and establishes what each icon stands for (its key value). Students read across the rows for Day 1 aloud together as a whole-class warm-up, practising the icon-to-number conversion before working independently.

Students complete Let Us Do Q1, p.208 ("Complete the table: total sold items for Fruit Chaats and Sandwiches across all three days.") independently, counting icons row by row and recording totals. Teacher watches for students who forget to multiply by the key value and prompts them to re-read the pictograph key.

Students answer Let Us Do Q2, p.208 ("On which day were the most sandwiches sold?") and Let Us Do Q3, p.208 ("Which item had the highest sale on Day 2?"), using their completed totals from Q1. Brief pair-check before the class confirms answers.

Students tackle Let Us Do Q4, p.208 ("Complete the total sales table (Day 1, Day 2, Day 3 combined) and circle the day that had the highest sales."), adding across both food types for each day. Teacher closes with a quick oral round: 'What made the pictograph useful here — what would have been harder without it?'

periods.teacher_notes: The most frequent error at this stage is reading icon count directly as the sales number without applying the key multiplier — insist students write 'icons × key value' before entering a total. Q2, Q3, and Q4 all depend on the correctly computed totals in Q1, so circulate to catch errors early.
materials: Rough paper for computing icon counts and totals

time_bands.activity: Quick oral revisit of survey-question design using Look at the questions asked by Rohan and Anjali, p.203 ("Tick the question that is the most appropriate for finding the 'most liked subject'...."). Two or three students justify their choice aloud, consolidating the idea that a well-framed question yields countable responses.

Students re-engage with Now look at the above table and answer the following questions, p.205 ("Identify the most common and least common favourite subject...."), this time asked to articulate in writing (one sentence) why the table is easier than the raw list. The writing act deepens the insight built through tallying 45 responses.

Students revisit Q1, p.206 ("Which colour ice gola do the children eat (a) the most and (b) the least? How do you know?") as a fluency check on pictograph reading. Pairs compare answers and must point to the specific icons that support their claim.

Students work on Answer these questions, p.207 ("Who plays Chess the most — Boys or Girls?....") using the class two-way table built from the survey of their own classmates. If the survey data is not available in their books, students use a teacher-drawn illustrative two-way table on the board.

Students complete Let Us Do Q4, p.208 ("Complete the total sales table (Day 1, Day 2, Day 3 combined) and circle the day that had the highest sales."), practising the icon-to-total computation under time pressure. Teacher takes a quick show of hands on the answer to confirm whole-class accuracy.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the ideas built across the whole chapter — well-framed survey questions, frequency tables, pictograph reading, two-way tables, and total computation — and is a good moment to surface and correct any persistent errors before formal assessment. A teacher-drawn illustrative two-way table on the board ensures the chess-cricket task is self-contained even when individual surveys were not recorded in students' books.
materials: Board and chalk or marker for illustrative two-way table if needed

items.section_title: Reading and interpreting a pictograph (Colourful Golas)
items.prompt: A pictograph shows four colours of golas: orange, green, yellow, and red. Rohan drew one human figure for each gola eaten by a boy, and Anjali drew one lolly icon for each gola eaten overall. Draw Anjali's pictograph for the following: Orange — 4 golas, Green — 6 golas, Yellow — 3 golas, Red — 5 golas. Use a simple circle to show each gola icon.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student draws 4 circles in the Orange row, 6 circles in the Green row, 3 circles in the Yellow row, and 5 circles in the Red row.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw one icon per item in the matching row, as shown in a pictograph.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them point to and count aloud before drawing; stretch: make their own pictograph for a different set of four colours.

exercise.book_ref: Look at the information given above, p.206
exercise.description: Colour the outline drawings of golas to match the colours shown in Rohan's and Anjali's data records.

items.section_title: Collecting and organising data in a two-way table (Chess or Cricket)
items.prompt:
Ten children were asked about the games they play. Here are their answers: Priya — chess only, Ravi — both, Meena — neither, Arjun — cricket only, Sita — chess only, Tarun — both, Kavya — cricket only, Dev — neither, Leela — chess only, Mohan — cricket only. Sort these children into the correct rows of the two-way table below.

Nature of Games | Children's names
Chess only | ___
Cricket only | ___
Both | ___
Neither | ___
items.visual_stimulus:
Nature of Games | Children's names
Chess only | ___
Cricket only | ___
Both | ___
Neither | ___

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Chess only: Priya, Sita, Leela. Cricket only: Arjun, Kavya, Mohan. Both: Ravi, Tarun. Neither: Meena, Dev.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read each child's answer and place the name in the matching category row.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them cut out name-cards and physically place them; stretch: add a Girls and Boys column and re-sort.

exercise.description: Find out from your classmates how many of them play only chess, only cricket, both or neither. Record in the space provided.

items.section_title: Framing a question and collecting data
items.prompt: A class wants to find out which one fruit each child likes the most. Which question should they ask?

options.label: B
options.text: How many fruits do you eat every day?

options.label: C
options.text: Which fruit do you like the most?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Which fruit do you like the most?
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A survey question that asks for one favourite produces a single, countable answer from each person.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not understood that the question must identify a specific favourite; a yes/no question gives no ranking.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses an open list-answer question with a single-favourite question; multiple answers cannot be easily tallied into one winner.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is thinking about quantity eaten rather than preference, missing the purpose of identifying the most liked fruit.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to act out answering each option and see which gives one clear answer; stretch: write one more good question and one bad question for a different survey topic.

exercise.book_ref: Look at the questions asked by Rohan and Anjali, p.203
exercise.description: Tick the question that is the most appropriate for finding the 'most liked subject'. Why do you think so? Discuss with your friends and teacher.

items.section_title: Organising data into a frequency table
items.prompt: A class voted for their favourite colour. The results are listed below in random order: Red, Blue, Red, Green, Blue, Red, Green, Blue, Red, Blue, Green, Red, Blue, Red, Blue. Raj counted and made a frequency table. He says Red has the most votes. Without counting again, explain how the frequency table makes it easy to check whether Raj is right.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A frequency table shows each colour and its count in one glance, so you can compare the numbers directly without scanning through the whole list. Red = 6, Blue = 6, Green = 3 — Red and Blue are tied, so Raj is not fully correct.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Tally the list into a frequency table, then compare the counts across rows.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to tally on their fingers first before looking at the table; stretch: ask what they would change in Raj's claim to make it accurate.

exercise.book_ref: Now look at the above table and answer the following questions, p.205
exercise.description: Identify the most common and least common favourite subject. Then decide which of the two ways of displaying information (raw list vs. table) is easier to understand and why.

items.section_title: Reading and interpreting a pictograph (Colourful Golas)
items.prompt: A pictograph shows golas eaten by children. Each icon stands for 1 gola. The number of icons for each colour is: Pink — 7, Yellow — 4, Orange — 9, Green — 5. Which colour gola was eaten the most and which was eaten the least?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Most: Orange (9 icons); Least: Yellow (4 icons).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the icons for each colour and compare to find the largest and smallest totals.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student picked the first colour listed as 'most' rather than counting icons, showing they did not read the pictograph carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student correctly identified 'most' but confused least with Green (5) instead of Yellow (4), suggesting they compared only some of the values.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student reversed the comparison, indicating confusion about which direction 'most' and 'least' point in a count.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to write the number next to each colour name before comparing; stretch: ask by how many more Orange was eaten than Yellow.

exercise.description: Which colour ice gola do the children eat (a) the most and (b) the least? How do you know?

items.section_title: Reading and interpreting a pictograph (Colourful Golas)
items.prompt: Rohan's pictograph shows boys' and girls' gola choices separately using human figures. Anjali's pictograph combines both boys and girls using lolly icons. Kavya wants to find out which colour girls prefer. Which pictograph — Rohan's or Anjali's — should she use? Explain why.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Kavya should use Rohan's pictograph because it separates boys' and girls' data. Anjali's pictograph combines everyone together, so girls' preferences cannot be read from it alone.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose the representation that keeps the needed category (girls) separate from others.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to describe what each pictograph shows before deciding; stretch: ask which pictograph to use if you wanted to compare total consumption across all children.

exercise.description: Which of the ways of representing data did you use to answer these questions and why?

items.section_title: Collecting and organising data in a two-way table (Chess or Cricket)
items.prompt: A two-way table shows: Chess only — 3 Girls, 5 Boys; Cricket only — 4 Girls, 2 Boys; Both — 2 Girls, 2 Boys; Neither — 1 Girl, 1 Boy. Who plays Cricket the most — Boys or Girls?
items.visual_stimulus:
Nature of Games | No. of Girls | No. of Boys
Chess only | 3 | 5
Cricket only | 4 | 2
Both | 2 | 2
Neither | 1 | 1

options.label: A
options.text: Boys and Girls are equal in cricket

options.label: C
options.text: Boys, because more boys are in the table overall

options.label: D
options.text: Girls, because 4 girls play cricket only, compared to 2 boys

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Girls play Cricket the most — 4 girls play cricket only, compared to 2 boys.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the Cricket only row and compare the Girls and Boys columns.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student read the wrong row (Chess only) and confused chess with cricket, showing they did not locate the correct row.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have added rows incorrectly or confused 'both' with cricket-only, failing to isolate the cricket-only row.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student compared overall totals rather than reading a specific row, showing they have not understood the two-way table's row-based comparison.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to trace a finger along the Cricket only row before answering; stretch: ask how many children in total (boys and girls combined) play cricket only.

exercise.description: Answer: (1) Who plays Chess the most — Boys or Girls? (2) Who plays Cricket the most — Boys or Girls? (3) How many children play both types of games?

items.section_title: Reading a pictograph and computing totals (Bal Mela)
items.prompt: A pictograph shows sandwich sales at a Bal Mela. Each icon stands for 5 sandwiches. Day 1 has 3 icons, Day 2 has 5 icons, Day 3 has 4 icons. On which day were the most sandwiches sold?

options.label: A
options.text: Day 1, because 3 icons means 15, which is a round number

options.label: C
options.text: Day 2, because it has the most icons

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Day 2, because it has 5 icons, meaning 5 × 5 = 25 sandwiches — the highest of the three days.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the icons per day, multiply by the key value, and compare to find the largest total.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student used position (first day) rather than data to decide, showing they did not read the pictograph.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student made a rough visual comparison without counting, confusing 'close to most' with 'the most'.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student introduced an irrelevant criterion (round number) instead of comparing icon counts, showing misunderstanding of how to use the key.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to write the number of sandwiches next to each day's icons before comparing; stretch: ask how many more sandwiches Day 2 sold than Day 1.

exercise.description: On which day were the most sandwiches sold?

items.section_title: Reading a pictograph and computing totals (Bal Mela)
items.prompt: At a school fair, fruit chaats and sandwiches were sold on Day 2. A pictograph shows: Fruit Chaats — 6 icons (each icon = 2 chaats); Sandwiches — 4 icons (each icon = 5 sandwiches). Which item had the higher sale on Day 2? Show how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Fruit Chaats: 6 × 2 = 12. Sandwiches: 4 × 5 = 20. Sandwiches had the higher sale on Day 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each item's icon count by its key value, then compare the two totals.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give them the multiplication as a fill-in sentence (6 × 2 = ___, 4 × 5 = ___) to scaffold; stretch: ask by how many more sandwiches outsold fruit chaats.

exercise.description: Which item had the highest sale on Day 2?

items.section_title: Organising data into a frequency table
items.prompt: A class of 20 children was asked their favourite sport. The raw list is: Football, Cricket, Football, Kabaddi, Cricket, Football, Kabaddi, Football, Cricket, Football, Football, Kabaddi, Cricket, Football, Cricket, Football, Kabaddi, Cricket, Football, Cricket. How many children like Football the most?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8 children like Football the most. (Tallying: Football — 8, Cricket — 7, Kabaddi — 5; total = 20.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count each occurrence of Football in the raw list using a tally.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student undercounted by one, likely missing one occurrence when scanning the list.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student overcounted by one, likely counting a Cricket or Kabaddi entry as Football.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student stopped counting too early or made two undercounting errors.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give them a printed list and let them cross out each Football as they count; stretch: complete a full frequency table for all three sports.

exercise.book_ref: Look at the children's responses above and answer the following questions, p.204
exercise.description: Fill in: the number of children who like Mathematics / Language / The World Around Us / Physical Education / Arts the most.

items.section_title: Collecting and organising data in a two-way table (Chess or Cricket)
items.prompt: Eight children were surveyed. Results: Anil — chess only, Bina — both, Charu — neither, Devi — cricket only, Elan — chess only, Fiza — cricket only, Gita — both, Hari — neither. In a two-way table, how many children are in the 'Both' row?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2 children — Bina and Gita — are in the 'Both' row.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Scan the survey results and count only those whose answer is 'both'.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counted only one of the two 'both' responses, likely stopping after finding the first.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have included a 'neither' or 'chess only' entry in the 'both' row by misreading.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have added 'both' and 'neither' together or miscounted across all categories.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask them to underline the word 'both' in each child's answer before counting; stretch: complete the full two-way table with a Girls and Boys column.

exercise.book_ref: Now let us organise the above data in the table, p.207
exercise.description: Fill the two-way table: rows Chess only / Cricket only / Both / Neither; columns No. of Girls and No. of Boys.

items.section_title: Reading a pictograph and computing totals (Bal Mela)
items.prompt: A pictograph shows fruit chaat sales over three days. Each icon stands for 3 chaats. Day 1 has 4 icons, Day 2 has 6 icons, Day 3 has 5 icons. What is the total number of fruit chaats sold across all three days?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the icon counts across all days, then multiply the total by the key value.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student added the icon counts (4+6+5=15) but forgot to multiply by the key value of 3.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have multiplied only two days' icons by 3, omitting one day, or used a key value of 2.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have added only Day 1 and Day 2 icons and multiplied by 3 (10×3=30 is incorrect here, suggesting they multiplied by a wrong factor or used 6 icons total).

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give them the sentence frame '___icons × 3 = ___ chaats' for each day before totalling; stretch: ask which day sold the most and by how many more than the least-selling day.

exercise.description: Complete the table: total sold items for Fruit Chaats and Sandwiches across all three days.

items.section_title: Reading a pictograph and computing totals (Bal Mela)
items.prompt: A sales table shows: Day 1 — 18 fruit chaats and 20 sandwiches; Day 2 — 24 fruit chaats and 15 sandwiches; Day 3 — 12 fruit chaats and 25 sandwiches. What is the total number of items sold across all three days combined?
items.visual_stimulus:
Day | Fruit Chaats | Sandwiches
Day 1 | 18 | 20
Day 2 | 24 | 15
Day 3 | 12 | 25

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sum each column separately, then add the two column totals together.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them add each column on their fingers or using a number line before combining; stretch: circle the day with the highest combined sales and find how much more it sold than the lowest day.

exercise.description: Complete the total sales table (Day 1, Day 2, Day 3 combined) and circle the day that had the highest sales.
